name: R-1,3-butanediol

lead: R-1,3-butanediol is the (R) form of a four-carbon diol that the body converts into beta-hydroxybutyrate. It appears in the exogenous ketone field as a precursor and as a component of some ketone esters, used with appetite control and fat loss in mind.

Wikipedia's ketone ester article states it raises blood ketones, by about 60 percent relative to the monoester, and notes that exogenous ketones lower blood glucose and may reduce ghrelin. The sources reviewed contain no trial testing it for fat loss or appearance.

paras: It is used as a liquid or as an ingredient in ketone drinks, typically alongside low-carb eating or fasting. It is not the same as 1,4-butanediol, which converts to GHB.

1,3-butanediol is recognized by the US FDA as a safe food ingredient (21 CFR 172.712), per Wikipedia. Pure chemical hazard notes include eye irritation. A study of a ketone diester in professional cyclists reported impaired time-trial performance.

angle.text: R-1,3-butanediol is converted to beta-hydroxybutyrate and raises blood ketones, with lower hunger and fat loss as the hoped-for payoff. Human evidence for fat loss or appearance has not been established.

lead: 1,3-Butanediol (C4H10O2) is a diol and secondary alcohol, a bittersweet water-soluble liquid used as a solvent, flavor-additive carrier, and intermediate for resins. The (R) enantiomer has CAS number 6290-03-5.[1] In the exogenous ketone field, R-1,3-butanediol is described as a compound that significantly raises blood ketone levels and is a component of ketone esters developed at the NIH by Richard Veech and Todd King.[2]

The US FDA recognizes 1,3-butanediol as a safe food ingredient under 21 CFR 172.712.[1] The Wikipedia article describes preliminary study of it for exercise recovery and as a possible oral ketone agent in anorexia nervosa research, but states that high production cost limits adoption.[1]
The sources reviewed contain no controlled trial of R-1,3-butanediol for fat loss or physical appearance.
infobox: Recognized as a food ingredient (21 CFR 172.712)

paras: 1,3-Butanediol is made by aldol condensation of acetaldehyde followed by catalytic hydrogenation, and it occurs naturally in bell peppers. Without an R or S label the compound is racemic.[1]

Wikipedia's ketone ester article lists R-1,3-butanediol among exogenous ketone agents, says it should not be confused with 1,4-butanediol (which converts to GHB), and notes that racemic diesters of the compound were tested in deep-sea divers and that C6 and C8 diesters with it are sold by Juvenescence Labs.[2] Exogenous ketones are reported to lower blood glucose and may reduce ghrelin.[2]

The same Wikipedia article reports that R-1,3-butanediol was tested once for sports performance and that time to fatigue was not significantly different.[2] A 2017 study of a ketone diester in professional cyclists reported impaired time-trial performance.[3] A registered healthy-volunteer study compared the effects of different ketone supplements on blood beta-hydroxybutyrate and glucose.[4] Registered trials of ketone supplementation in frailty, alcohol use disorder and sleep apnea are under way or suspended; none concerns appearance.[5][6]

Animal work with ketone esters includes a mouse study reporting increased brown adipose tissue mitochondrial biogenesis and UCP1 on a ketone ester diet, and a 2014 mouse study of ketone supplementation in metastatic cancer.[7][8] These are not human appearance outcomes.
